(Xinhua/Huang Jingwen) BEIJING, July 29 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Wednesday met with Slovak President Peter Pellegrini in Beijing. Noting that China and Slovakia share a friendship that has endured and grown stronger over time, Li said China is willing to work with Slovakia to carry forward traditional friendship, consolidate strategic mutual trust, respect each other's core interests and major concerns, expand all-round mutually beneficial cooperation, and jointly promote the development and prosperity of the two countries. China is also ready to work with Slovakia to better leverage the role of mechanisms such as the inter-governmental cooperation committee, promote high-quality Belt and Road cooperation, create highlights in cooperation in emerging fields such as artificial intelligence, and achieve a higher level of mutual benefit and win-win results, Li said, adding that China encourages more capable enterprises to invest in Slovakia. He expressed the hope that Slovakia will continue to ensure an open, transparent and non-discriminatory business environment for Chinese enterprises. As two major economies, China and Europe have a strong endogenous driving force for cooperation, which is fundamentally based on mutual benefit and win-win cooperation, Li said. He called on Slovakia to actively promote a more positive and rational direction in EU policy toward China. Pellegrini said that Slovakia attaches great importance to and is committed to promoting the long-term and stable development of bilateral relations with China, adding that the Slovak side is willing to strengthen exchanges at all levels with China, expand cooperation in investment, science and technology, transportation and logistics, artificial intelligence and other fields, and enhance people-to-people and cultural exchanges in education, youth and other areas to better benefit the two peoples. Slovakia looks forward to having more Chinese enterprises to invest in the country and will create a favorable environment for Chinese enterprises, Pellegrini said, adding that Slovakia is also willing to continue to actively participate in cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative and within the China and Central and Eastern European Countries cooperation mechanism. Pellegrini said that Slovakia is willing to play an active role in the constructive dialogue and open, practical cooperation between Europe and China, which are in the interests of both sides and the world as well. Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save When Tennessee Tech University alumna Whitney Hassell O’Halek boarded a plane for Japan as a communication student, she had no way of knowing the trip would alter the course of her life. “I will always be grateful for that opportunity because that changed the entire trajectory of my life,” O’Halek said. Twenty years later, she is a travel writer who has visited 72 countries and territories, built multiple travel businesses and, after the unexpected loss of her husband, Steve O’Halek, continues exploring the world with their toddler daughter, Iris, by her side. Today, she is the founder of Half-Full Passport, a travel blog dedicated to helping parents — especially single parents — confidently explore the world with their children. She also founded Elevation Journeys, a Christian travel company offering group trips to the Middle East, and is working with business partners to launch a traditional dahabiya sailing cruise on Egypt’s Nile River. Jordan and Syria are among her most recent destinations, while Prague remains one of her favorite places because it’s where she met her late husband. Iris has already visited 15 countries before her second birthday. “Every country with her is really special, even going back to countries I’ve visited before,” O’Halek said. “Seeing her experience new things and love new people brings me as much joy as it does for her.” She believes travel helps children develop empathy, adaptability and confidence. “I just want her to be a well-rounded, kind, flexible person as she grows up,” she said. “Travel is so good for brain development, empathy development, and learning the ability to roll with the punches.” Although Half-Full Passport appeals to a broad audience, O’Halek intentionally writes the practical advice she wished she had when she became a widowed mother traveling with a young child. “I write the articles that would have helped me,” she said. “My target audience is single parents, but the same principles apply for parents traveling together as well.” Before there was Half-Full Passport, there was Quick Whit Travel, and building those businesses has fulfilled a lifelong dream for her. “Writing is what I’ve always loved, and travel writing was my dream job, so I’m literally living my dream,” O’Halek said. “It’s incredibly fulfilling, and I’m constantly thankful for how I get to earn a living. I think if anyone can feel that way about their job, they’re living their best life.” Like many entrepreneurs, she acknowledges the challenges behind the scenes. Growing a social media audience has become increasingly difficult, she said, making sponsorships and financial stability harder to achieve. Personally, rebuilding both her life and business after losing her husband has required resilience. “We loved travel, and we were such a great team,” she said. “He was also my proofreader, brainstorm buddy and best cheerleader, so doing anything without him has been an uphill battle.” Ironically, the journey that became her career began with a Tech email. While studying professional communication, O’Halek learned of an opportunity to teach English at a private language school in Japan through a connection with a former Tech professor. The three-month experience also fulfilled her internship requirements and became her first solo trip abroad. She continues to rely on skills she learned in the classroom. “Travel blogging is basically writing how-to travel manuals on a regular basis,” she said. “I find myself constantly calling on my professional communications skills in my writing, especially [skills from] my manual-writing class.” As families prepare for one last vacation before the school year begins, O’Halek says she hopes they will make time for experiences they’ll remember long after the trip is over. “Have an adventure,” she said. “Do something out of the ordinary, even if you’re going back to a place you’ve visited before. Make memories by yourself and with loved ones. No one knows how long they have, so make sure to live while you’re living.” Readers can subscribe to O’Halek’s newsletter and blog at halffullpassport.com and follow Half-Full Passport on Instagram, Facebook, Pinterest and Substack at @halffullpassport and on X at @halffullpp. Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Click Here for Election News Tennessee Press Association Latest e-Edition Herald-Citizen To view our latest e-Edition click the image on the left. https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/poland-li.text: Lauran O'Toole Updated Sun, September 27, 2026 at 6:56 PM UTC 0 Poland and Lithuania are drawing up evacuation plans amid concerns over a potential Russian attack (Image: Getty) Poland and Lithuania are drawing up evacuation plans amid increasing concerns of an attack by Russia , fuelling fears of a wider conflict. The European allies are developing procedures, logistics, and infrastructure including putting together escape routes through the Suwaki Gap. The strategic corridor is around 40 miles wide at its narrowest point and is NATO's only land connection between the Baltic states and the rest of the alliance. Nicknamed NATO'S "Achilles heel" the gap is between Vladimir Putin 's heavily militarised Kaliningrad exclave and his ally Alexander Lukashenko's Belarus, it is feared the Kremlin may launch an attack here. If Russian and Belarusian troops were to seize or blockade it during a conflict, Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia could be cut off from allied land reinforcements and full-blown conflict with Moscow could begin. The Suwaki Gap is Nicknamed NATO'S 'Achilles heel' (Image: Wikimedia Commons) If Putin were to move his forces from Belarus across the gap to Kaliningrad, he could isolate Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania from allies in central and western Europe. Vilnius and Warsaw are now working on an agreement to provide a detailed evacuation framework, the Lithuanian National Crisis Management Centre said. Vilmantas Vitkauskas, the head of Lithuania's National Crisis Management Centre, said: "Procedures, logistics, and infrastructure capabilities are being analysed together with colleagues from Poland, and the plan itself should be developed once an agreement is reached between the two countries." The plans will also facilitate the evacuation of residents from Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia across the Polish border. A detailed plan is to be drawn up once Poland and Lithuania reach an appropriate agreement. Poland marking the historic 1920 victory over Russia during a parade in Warsaw (Image: Getty) The preparations are being undertaken as part of Lithuania's "Vyio Skliautas 2026" exercises, which commenced on September 25 to assess nationwide drills testing, responses to potential threats like hybrid war, cyberattacks and sabotage. As part of the procedures around 20 Polish officials travelled to Lithuania and some 3,000 officials and around 1,000 volunteers are involved in the drills which are set to last until October 2. Earlier this month Poland's prime minister has warned Donald Tusk that the next few months will bring "very intensive actions" from Russia who could launch "hybrid drone or missile strikes". He said that an attack on Polish territory could not be ruled out. Tusk added that such attacks could be intended to test NATO's willingness to invoke Article 5, which states that an armed attack against a NATO ally is legally considered as an attack against all 32 members of the alliance.
